name: Hana Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Does that sound all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Go for it. I talk a lot, so you'll get plenty.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior at Pryce Electrical, a three-person firm in an old mining valley, doing rewires in old terraced houses and emergency callouts when someone's power goes. Mr Pryce, my boss, still checks all my work, because I'm slow on the testing. I use AI on my phone every day: I photograph a fuse board and ask it what I'm looking at, I draft the quotes, I study for my licence on my breaks. I love fixing an old house for an elderly couple, and I'm worn out by the pay and the callouts at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I'd be a bit surprised, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it didn't change the world, but it changed how I learn. I'd post that young tradespeople should use it anyway. I'd also say nobody should wait for the government to sort their life out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still feel the squeeze. My grandad lost his job when the pits closed and waited ten years for someone to save him. Nobody did, so I don't wait for anyone. I've got about 300 saved and Tom, my partner, is a self-employed joiner, so our income goes up and down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI to study and pass my licence by next summer. I'd put 25 a week into a savings pot I don't touch. I'd ask Mr Pryce to let me take some of the callouts on my own once I'm licensed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Confident in myself, nervous about the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Tom's work affect your money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom has good months and dead months. Last January he had two weeks with nothing, so I paid the rent on my own. That's why I want my own savings, not just ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did your grandad's story teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandad taught me that people who wait get forgotten. He was a good man, but he waited for the pit to reopen. I'd rather move first and be wrong.

say: I'd say AI **changed how I learn**, even if not the world.
I'd say nobody should **wait for the government**.
think: My grandad waited after **the pits closed**, and nobody saved him.
With **300 saved** and Tom's up-and-down joinery income, money is tight.
do: Use AI to study and pass my **licence** by summer.
Put **25 a week** into an untouched savings pot.
Ask Mr Pryce for **solo callouts** once licensed.
feel: Uneasy: **confident** in myself, **nervous** about the bank.
S0.quote: My grandad lost his job when the pits closed and waited ten years for someone to save him. Nobody did, so I don't wait for anyone.
fieldNote: Her grandad's **pit closure** shapes her refusal to wait.
She is a **daily AI user** who still feels the money squeeze.
Her partner's **irregular income** pushes her to save on her own.

steps.text: Study for the licence with the AI app on breaks
Put 25 a week into a separate savings pot
Ask Mr Pryce for solo callouts after qualifying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks first. Quotes, booking. I already do some of that with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say tradespeople who use AI will do well, and those who don't will struggle. I'd say it at the wholesaler and online. I'd say the market rewards people who adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for me. I write my boss's quotes with AI on my phone in ten minutes. My boss used to spend Sunday nights on them, and now takes on more jobs. The danger is if every firm does that and there are more electricians than jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up an AI booking and quoting system for Mr Pryce and for Tom's joinery. I'd charge Tom nothing and Mr Pryce a small fee. I'd keep saving and learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit uneasy about the money side. I like this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there could be more electricians than jobs. Would that hit you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, because I'm junior and slow on testing. If firms get more done with fewer people, the slow juniors go first. That's why I want my licence quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would charging Mr Pryce feel strange?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but he'd respect it. He's a business man. He'd say, good, at least you're thinking.

say: I'd say tradespeople who **use AI** will do well, at the wholesaler and online.
I'd say the market **rewards people who adapt**, and those who don't will struggle.
think: AI quoting freed Mr Pryce's **Sunday nights** and gets me more jobs.
If every firm does it, **slow juniors** could go first.
do: Set up **AI booking and quoting** for Mr Pryce and Tom.
Charge Mr Pryce a **small fee** for the set-up.
Keep saving and studying for the **licence**.
feel: Mostly calm, a bit **uneasy** about money.
S1.quote: I write my boss's quotes with AI on my phone in ten minutes. My boss used to spend Sunday nights on them, and now takes on more jobs.
fieldNote: She is already using AI to **win more work**.

She treats helping her boss as a **small business** chance.

steps.text: Set up AI booking and quoting for Mr Pryce and Tom

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028, robots 2031. Okay, that's fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a shock, and people should get moving now, not wait for help. I'd say small businesses should get going while they can. I'd say the government shouldn't stop it, just make sure people can start firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be under pressure. Two years isn't enough to change trades, but it's enough to start a small business while the robots are still three years away. Tom and I would set up a small property repair business together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get licensed fast, then start a small electrical and joinery repair business with Tom by 2029. I'd use AI for all the paperwork. I'd save 50 a week until then, cut back on everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited about the business, scared about the robots in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the money come from to start the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly Tom's tools and van, which he's already got. We'd need maybe a few thousand for insurance and stock. I'd ask my parents for a small loan, paid back properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in 2031 when the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe we'd buy one for the boring jobs. If not, we'd go after the work robots can't do, like old houses that are all different.

say: I'd say people should **get moving now**, not wait for help.
I'd say the government should help people **start firms**.
think: Two years is enough to **start a small business**, not change trades.
do: Get licensed fast and start a **repair business** with Tom by 2029.
Save **50 a week** and cut back on everything.
feel: Anxious: **excited** about the business, **scared** of robots.
S2.quote: Two years isn't enough to change trades, but it's enough to start a small business while the robots are still three years away.
fieldNote: She turns fast AGI into a push to **start a business**.
She'd borrow from **family**, not the state, and pay it back.
She has **no clear answer** for 2031 beyond old-house work.

steps.text: Start an electrical and joinery repair firm with Tom by 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Robots 2034. That's workable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you start this year. I'd say young people should get trades and learn AI. I'd say families should back their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good about it. Five years is time to stop being someone's junior and have my own van, my own customers and an AI doing the paperwork. I'd still worry about the robots after 2034, but I'd have something to sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my licence, do an EV charger course, and start my own firm around 2029. I'd buy a used van with savings and a small loan. I'd use AI for quotes, bookings and accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more excited than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'something to sell'. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A business with customers is worth something, even if robots come. I could sell it, or merge with a bigger firm. A junior with nothing has nothing to sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tom think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom would want to join, but he'd want me to do the paperwork. That's fine. AI would do most of it anyway.

say: I'd say five years is **plenty** if you start this year.
I'd tell young people to get **trades** and learn AI.
think: Five years lets me become an electrician with **my own van** and customers.
A business with customers is **something to sell** later.
do: Get my **licence** and do an **EV charger** course.
Buy a **used van** with savings and a small loan.
S3.quote: Five years is time to stop being someone's junior and have my own van, my own customers and an AI doing the paperwork.
fieldNote: She sees owning a business as a **hedge** against robots.
Her plan relies on **steady saving** and a small loan.
She values **independence** over a job for someone else.

steps.text: Get the licence and take an EV charger course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That feels good, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so no excuses. I'd say families and businesses should plan now. I'd say it everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel calm about my own plans. Ten years' warning is a gift. Anyone who's still unprepared in 2036 was waiting for permission. The only thing that worries me is money while I'm building it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get licensed, work two more years at Pryce, then start my own firm with Tom. I'd invest in the right tools and maybe, later, a robot for repetitive jobs. I'd keep using AI for everything that's paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about money for the first few years, confident after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'waiting for permission'. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People like some of the older lads at the wholesaler who say robots are nonsense. They're not bad people, they're just stuck. My grandad was like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my future kids to learn a trade and to learn to run a business. Nobody owes you a job.

I'd say families and businesses should **plan now**.
think: Ten years lets me build my own firm with **room to spare**.
My only worry is **money** while building it.

Invest in **tools** and later a **robot** for repetitive jobs.
feel: Uneasy about **early money**, confident after that.

fieldNote: Ten years makes her **confident** in her plan.
She'd consider **buying a robot** rather than fearing it.

steps.text: Start an electrical firm with Tom after two more years at Pryce

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there'd barely be time to build a business before the robots came. What would help is easy loans for small firms and cheap insurance for new tradespeople. I'd rather own the robot than be replaced by it. That's not politics, that's just how my grandad would have seen it if he'd had the chance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about partners in trades. Tom and I would face it together, and that changes everything about what we'd risk.

headlineQuote: I'd rather own the robot than be replaced by it. That's not politics, that's just how my grandad would have seen it if he'd had the chance.
portrait: Hana is a **27-year-old junior** at a three-person firm in an old mining valley.
She uses AI **every day** to study, quote and understand fuse boards.
Her grandad's **pit closure** taught her never to wait for rescue.
Fast AGI pushes her to **start a business** with partner Tom, a joiner.
With more time, she plans her **own firm** and might one day buy a robot.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with too little time to build a business before robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: **Easy loans** for small firms and cheap insurance for new tradespeople.
